---
title: "How Build Works"
---

Build is Revolte's implementation layer. It takes a high-level requirement, analyzes the connected repository, and produces a reviewable software change with code, tests, and documentation where needed.

The important distinction is control. Revolte can generate the implementation, but Build hands the result back as a pull request so your team can inspect, refine, approve, and merge it using your normal engineering process.

## Why Build exists

Teams lose time translating product intent into repetitive implementation work: wiring routes, writing validation, adding tests, updating docs, and preparing pull requests. Build compresses that cycle while preserving review.

Use Build to:

- Move from requirement to implementation faster
- Keep generated changes aligned with the existing codebase
- Standardize tests and documentation around new work
- Reduce manual setup for routine feature delivery
- Preserve human approval before code merges

## How it works

<Steps>
  <Step title="Requirement analysis">
    Revolte interprets the requested behavior and identifies the application areas likely to change.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Repository understanding">
    Revolte reads the connected codebase to learn framework conventions, folder structure, testing patterns, and runtime configuration.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Implementation planning">
    The request is broken into scoped technical tasks so the output stays reviewable.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Generation and validation">
    Revolte edits code, adds tests, and runs validation where the project setup allows it.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Pull request delivery">
    The result is delivered as a pull request with a summary of the change and validation evidence.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## When to use Build

Build is best for changes with clear behavior and reviewable scope.

| Use case | Good fit? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add an API endpoint | Yes | Behavior, inputs, and tests can be specified clearly |
| Add a UI state | Yes | Revolte can follow existing component patterns |
| Fix a failing test | Yes | The failure provides concrete feedback |
| Large architecture rewrite | Use carefully | Break it into smaller requests |
| Undefined product exploration | Not first | Clarify the requirement before generating code |

## Inputs

Build starts with a requirement. The best inputs describe the outcome, constraints, and acceptance criteria.

Include:

- Business behavior
- API or UI contract
- Data model expectations
- Permission rules
- Error handling
- Testing expectations
- Existing files, routes, or patterns to preserve

## Outputs

Every successful build should produce a pull request that your team can review.

Typical outputs include:

- Source code changes
- Unit or integration tests
- Documentation updates
- Pull request summary
- Validation logs or check results
- Configuration changes when required by the feature

## Boundaries

Build accelerates implementation, but it does not replace engineering judgment. Review generated pull requests for correctness, maintainability, security, and deployment impact before merging.

> **Recommended practice**  
> Treat Revolte output like a teammate's pull request: review the diff, inspect tests, verify configuration, and merge only when the change satisfies the requirement.
